{"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_f00826ce58f54514","text":"Your March 30–April 12 records stayed close to your 28-day baseline. Sleep averaged 7h52m versus 7h51m, with starts at 22:42–22:57 and a consistent 07:00 wake time. Weekday and weekend sleep and steps were similar.

Steps averaged 7,923 versus 7,938, although they drifted down about 22/day within these two weeks. Active time increased slightly, from 54.7 to 56.2 minutes/day, mostly through higher weekday averages. Recorded activity continued around 21:00. Low movement averaged 447 versus 450 minutes/day but edged upward within the window; daytime bouts remained about 44–47 minutes with five-minute gaps.

Resting heart rate stayed near 62 bpm; RMSSD stayed near 45 ms with smaller daily fluctuations. There was little relationship between activity and sleep ending the following morning, or between heart rate and RMSSD. All days had valid recordings. These small shifts stayed within your baseline ranges, without a sustained departure."},{"case_ref":"sample_d0a5b6f2398d4ebc","text":"Your main change was an isolated RMSSD reading of 23 ms on April 5, compared with your baseline range of 43–47 ms. It returned to 43 ms the next day and stayed at 43–46 afterward. This reading pulled the two-week mean down from 45.3 to 43.1 ms, while the median remained 45 ms; it does not show a persistent decline or a recurring weekend pattern.

Resting heart rate averaged 55.8 versus 56.3 bpm, continuing a slight downward trend within the same 55–57 range. Sleep averaged 7h48m versus 7h51m, with starts about three minutes later and unchanged 07:00 wakes. The small baseline weekend sleep advantage nearly disappeared.

Steps were down 1.4% to 7,954/day; active time remained near 55 minutes, around 21:00, and low movement near 453 minutes. Activity had virtually no relationship with following-morning sleep. Heart rate and RMSSD were moderately inversely associated, but the isolated reading limits interpretation. Coverage was complete; monitoring whether that reading repeats would clarify persistence."},{"case_ref":"sample_e97142a55baea655","text":"Your recorded movement dropped abruptly and remained lower throughout March 30–April 12, across weekdays and weekends. Steps averaged 2,321 versus your 28-day baseline of 7,998, a 71% reduction. Active time fell from 55.2 to 4.9 minutes/day, down 91%, with no return toward baseline. The usual 21:00 activity intervals shortened from 50–60 to 0–10 minutes; two days recorded zero active minutes with complete wear coverage.

Other measures stayed close to baseline: low movement averaged 447.5 versus 450.5 minutes, sleep 7h49m versus 7h51m, resting heart rate 56.3 versus 56.1 bpm, and RMSSD 44.8 versus 45.3 ms. Sleep and RMSSD edged upward within the window. Sleep starts remained 22:42–22:58 with 07:00 wakes.

Activity had only a modest relationship with following-morning sleep (r=0.32, 13 pairs). Heart rate and RMSSD were inversely associated (r=-0.59), without establishing a cause. All recordings were valid. Continued recording can show whether the movement change persists."},{"case_ref":"sample_9e2cc57b2faef23c","text":"Your resting heart rate shifted upward at the start of March 30–April 12 and stayed elevated on every recorded day: 61–63 bpm versus your baseline range of 51–53. The average rose from 51.8 to 61.7 bpm, about 9.9 bpm or 19%. This was a sustained change across weekdays and weekends, with no return toward baseline.

RMSSD remained stable at 45.1 versus 44.8 ms, with smaller daily fluctuations, so it did not show a parallel sustained change. Sleep also stayed near baseline: 7h52m versus 7h51m, starts at 22:42–22:57, and consistent 07:00 wakes.

Steps averaged 7,923 versus 7,938, despite a slight downward trend within the window. Active time increased from 54.7 to 56.2 minutes/day around 21:00; low movement averaged 447 versus 450 minutes but edged upward. Weekday/weekend differences were small. Activity and following-morning sleep, and heart rate and RMSSD, had weak relationships. Coverage was complete. Tracking whether the heart-rate shift continues would clarify its duration; these records do not explain its cause."}]}
